title: Timeline-scrubbed animation (play, loop, speed): what happens over time?
summary: A strip of key frames sharing one clock, with a time slider, play, loop and speed controls. It teaches you to read an animation in print: frames are samples of one continuous history, and the slider says which one you are looking at.

media.alt: Four key frames of a travelling decaying wave at 0, 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 seconds, the third highlighted, above a time slider with play and loop buttons.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

read_the_figure.question: What happens over time?
read_the_figure.axes: Four panels at t = 0, 1.5, 3.0 and 4.5 s, each showing a travelling decaying wave on fixed axes (y from -1.3 to 1.3). The third frame is outlined in amber. Below: a timeline with ticks at the four times, a thumb at t = 3.0 s of 4.5 s, play and loop buttons, speed 1x.
look_at: Which frame is current (amber) and what time does the slider say?
How does the wave move and how does its amplitude change from frame to frame?
Are the axes the same in every frame?
What are the controls: play, loop and speed?
read_the_figure.proves: It shows the evolution of one field in time, with each key frame taken from the same clock. It does not show what happens between frames, which are samples.
if_wrong: Frames with different axis limits: shapes cannot be compared.
No time label on each frame: the order is unclear.
A timeline with no end time: the reader cannot tell how much is left.

terms.meaning: A sample of the animation at one time, shown as a still.
One clock that drives every view; the slider sets the time for all.
Dragging the slider to move forward and backward through the time series.
Replay from the start when the end is reached.
Playback rate relative to real time (1x is real time).

remember: Every frame carries its time (t = ... s).
Slider position / total time says how far you are.
Frames are samples: motion between them is interpolation by the eye.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each frame is a plot of the same quantity against position, so a line shape encodes the field at that moment. The amber outline and bold title mark the current frame; the other titles are plain. The timeline encodes time by position along a bar, with ticks at the frame times, an amber thumb at the current time and a label with current over total. Buttons show state by outline style (solid play, dashed loop).

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: An animation is a function of time. Showing the key frames side by side gives the whole story at once, which a moving picture does not; the slider and buttons give access to the continuous version. Using one clock for every view means that frames and annotations agree at every instant, which is why shared timeline is a rule of this class.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Which frame is current and what is the time? The third, outlined in amber, with t = 3.0 s, and the thumb is at 3.0 on a bar of 4.5 s (two thirds across). Q2: How does the wave move and decay? The crest moves right as time passes: the wave is sin(x - 1.3 t), a shift of 1.3 rad per second, so about 1.95 rad per frame; the amplitude drops to e^(-0.1 t) of the start: 0.86 at 1.5 s, 0.74 at 3.0 s and 0.64 at 4.5 s. Q3: Are the axes the same? Yes: each frame has y from -1.3 to 1.3 and no ticks, so the visible shrinking of the peak is real.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Shared timeline and time label: all views driven by one clock and each frame labelled with its time. Without them one cannot say that two pictures show the same instant.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Frames hide what happens between them: a fast event between 1.5 and 3.0 s would be missed. Axes that change from frame to frame, or an autoscaled amplitude, hide the decay; here the limits are fixed so the amplitude falls visibly (1.0, 0.86, 0.74, 0.64). Looping hides the start and the end. Speed above 1x changes how motion is perceived. Animated content is a problem for people who are sensitive to motion; a pause control and a static fallback matter.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Small multiples (this strip) with a common y axis; a space-time diagram (position against time as colour) shows the whole history in one picture; an overlay of several times on one plot with a colour per time.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Replace the strip by a space-time colour map with a vertical line at the current time, and add frame numbers and total frames beside the slider.

steps.title: Amplitude and phase at the key frames
steps.note: Between frames the wave shifts by 1.95 rad, about 0.31 of a wavelength.

worked.title: What the four frames should show
worked.problem: u = exp(-0.1 t) sin(x - 1.3 t). Find the amplitude at t = 0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.5 s, and the shift of the crest between consecutive frames.

solution.text: Shift between frames, as a fraction of the wavelength 2 pi.

worked.answer: Amplitude 1.00, 0.86, 0.74, 0.64; crest moves 0.31 wavelength per frame: a viewer can verify the render frame by frame.

checks.answer: Every frame and view is driven by one time value.

checks.q: Frames are 1.5 s apart and the wave speed is 1.3 rad/s. Phase shift per frame?
A reviewer says the wave does not decay because the peak looks the same height in two frames. What do you check?
checks.answer: Whether the axes are the same and fixed; if one frame is autoscaled the peaks look equal, so compare against the common limits.
